sections.0.body.0.t: CWPP (Cloud Workload Protection Platform) is the sensor inside the workload: VM, container, serverless function, Kubernetes host. CSPM looks at configuration; CWPP looks at behavior. It sees syscalls, network connections, processes, file reads, binary modification, and correlates that against rules and models.

sections.0.body.1.t: When everything goes right, CWPP does not show up: a rule detection log, a discreet alert in the SIEM, and the workload keeps running. When it goes wrong, it is the difference between a crypto miner running for six months and being cut off in three minutes.

sections.1.body.0.t: The classic choice is agent-based (a process that starts inside the workload and intercepts events) versus eBPF-based (programs running inside the kernel, with no extra process). Each has trade-offs.

sections.1.bullets.0.t: user-space agent (Falco, Aqua): broad visibility, easy to update, but it is one more attackable process

sections.1.bullets.1.t: eBPF (Tetragon, Falco with the eBPF driver, Datadog CWS): instruments the kernel directly, no extra process, but the rules end up limited to what the kernel exposes through hooks

sections.1.bullets.2.t: kernel module: maximum visibility, but compromises compatibility with managed kernels (GKE, optimized EKS)

sections.1.bullets.3.t: per-pod sidecar: isolates the sensor from the workload, useful when the workload cannot be modified, but costs more resources

sections.1.heading.t: How it works: agents and eBPF

sections.2.body.0.t: The rule does not ask 'which process is running?', it asks 'is this process doing something it has never done before?'. The classic form is a signature over syscalls: process, container, syscall, condition. The modern form is a behavior model (baseline per workload) that triggers on anomalies, not signatures.

sections.2.body.1.t: Falco is the open standard for signatures. The rule below catches the classic pattern of a shell being opened inside a container, something no legitimate application does in production:

sections.2.code.0.code.t:
- rule: Terminal shell in container
  desc: >
    Detect shell spawned inside a workload container.
    Legitimate workloads never open an interactive shell at runtime;
    this is a strong indicator of intrusion or hands-on-keyboard activity.
  condition: >
    container and
    spawned_process and
    proc.name in (shell_binaries)
  output: >
    shell=%proc.name parent=%proc.pname cmdline=%proc.cmdline
    container=%container.name image=%container.image.repository
    k8s=%k8s.ns.name/%k8s.pod.name
  priority: WARNING
  tags: [container, mitre_execution, mitre_T1059]

sections.2.heading.t: Behavioral detection: rules about what happens

sections.3.body.0.t: Detection without response is just noise. CWPP has three levers, in increasing order of aggressiveness:

sections.3.bullets.0.t: alert: sends an event to the SIEM/SOAR, a human decides. No change to the workload

sections.3.bullets.1.t: network isolation: a NetworkPolicy or security group starts blocking the pod/VM's egress, cutting exfiltration while keeping the process alive for forensics

sections.3.bullets.2.t: kill / quarantine: terminates the process, snapshots the filesystem for analysis, container removed. It is the right response when the rule is certainty (not anomaly)

sections.4.body.0.t: CWPP lives after the deploy. It assumes CSPM did its part (configuration OK), containers were hardened (runtime OK), and now the question is: what is happening in here? It plugs into the SIEM alongside CloudTrail, VPC flow logs and endpoint EDR for correlation (shell in the container + STS AssumeRole token in the same 30s window = critical incident).

sections.5.bullets.0.t: detects what no configuration catches: zero-day in a legitimate process, exfiltration over an allowed channel, persistence on a clean filesystem

sections.5.bullets.1.t: behavior-based rules catch families of attacks, not a specific CVE: a reverse shell in any language triggers the same rule

sections.5.bullets.2.t: preserved evidence: the filesystem snapshot taken after detection supports the incident investigation

sections.6.bullets.0.t: an agent inside the workload is new surface: a bug in the sensor becomes RCE inside the node, and history has examples

sections.6.bullets.1.t: telemetry cost at scale: instrumenting a thousand containers with eBPF looks free until the log volume reaches the SIEM, where the ingestion cost shows up

sections.6.bullets.2.t: behavioral false positives break trust: a rule that is too good is a rule everyone silences; tuning is permanent work, not a one-time setup

tagline.t: Cloud Workload Protection Platform watches what happens inside the VM, container and serverless function: syscalls, connections and processes, at execution time.
